module_title: Foundation Model Customization, Evaluation and Bedrock Applications
part_title: RAG, Knowledge Bases and Vector Search
review_basis: Visually inspected original numbered WebP slides 15 through 20 individually in order; verified RAG pipelines, S3 versus vector index, service comparisons, connector changes, citation examples, and review boundaries.

scenes.title: RAG with Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases
scenes.narration: This slide introduces retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, using a real company warranty question. Follow the five numbered panels from left to right. The user asks, 'What does our warranty cover for a laptop battery?' In panel two, Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases retrieves three relevant pieces of documentation: the warranty policy, battery coverage information, and exclusions for misuse. These pieces are called chunks, which simply means smaller portions of source documents. Panel three combines the original question with those retrieved passages into an augmented prompt. Notice that the model receives the actual warranty statements, rather than having to guess from its training. In panel four, a foundation model in Amazon Bedrock writes a response using that context. Panel five shows an answer explaining defects in materials and workmanship, battery coverage during the warranty period, and the exclusion for misuse. The numbered citation markers point back to each source. Now look at the bottom-left ingestion diagram, because it explains how those source chunks become searchable. Documents such as policies and guides are split into chunks, converted to numerical embeddings that represent meaning, and stored in a vector index. The green reminder below says the model's weights remain unchanged: RAG provides extra information when a question is asked, rather than retraining the model. The purple reminder warns that freshness depends on ingestion and synchronization. A newly changed policy is not automatically searchable until the update has been processed. Finally, a citation helps us trace an answer but does not guarantee it is correct. For an important warranty decision, check the actual cited clause.

scenes.title: RAG architecture: S3 to a grounded answer
scenes.narration: This slide makes the architecture of RAG very clear by dividing it into two horizontal lanes. Start with the upper ingestion lane. At the left, Amazon S3 stores the original PDFs and documents. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases then parses those files, splits long text into manageable chunks, and attaches source metadata such as file identity. Next, an embedding model, illustrated with the purple brain, converts each chunk into a vector, a list of numbers that captures semantic relationships. The vector store on the far right keeps those embeddings and metadata for similarity search. The example store shown is OpenSearch Serverless; the supported choice depends on configuration. Now move to the lower runtime lane. A user asks a natural-language question. A compatible embedding model represents that question numerically, so the search can find nearby document vectors. Look at the yellow outline: the Retrieve operation returns relevant chunks, then the question and chunks can be sent to a generative foundation model in Amazon Bedrock. The model produces the answer and links to the original documents. The yellow label RetrieveAndGenerate shows a managed operation that combines retrieval and answer generation, while Retrieve alone returns source chunks for your application to handle. Notice the small key-component cards at the bottom. S3 stores documents, Knowledge Bases manages processing and retrieval, and the vector store supports similarity search. These are different roles, not interchangeable storage products. A useful question is: if we upload a revised document to S3 but never synchronize the index, will search reliably use its new information? No. The ingestion lane must process the change.

scenes.title: Why RAG uses a vector store
scenes.narration: The title asks why RAG uses a vector store, so follow the five-stage diagram from left to right. First, source documents such as PDFs, web pages and policies live in an Amazon S3 bucket. Read the note directly below the bucket: ordinary S3 storage for the original files is not itself the vector index. Second, documents are divided into smaller text chunks. The examples on screen are Introduction, Security roles and Access control. An embedding model converts each chunk into a numerical vector. Those bracketed numbers are illustrative coordinates in an embedding space, not the actual content of a security policy. Third, a vector store records the embeddings alongside the original text chunks and source metadata, such as file name, page and URL. Fourth, a user asks 'How do I configure access control?' The question is embedded with a compatible model, and similarity search identifies relevant chunks, including access-control policies, IAM roles and permissions examples. Finally, the language model uses that retrieved context to answer, with a source such as guide dot docx, page one. This is semantic retrieval: it can find related meaning even when the user does not type the exact document wording. But similarity does not prove that an answer is correct or that the user is authorized to view the document. Now glance at the AWS options along the bottom: OpenSearch Service, Aurora PostgreSQL with vector support, S3 Vectors, and Neptune Analytics for certain graph-oriented cases. Each offers different indexing and integration capabilities. The right choice depends on the retrieval workload and AWS support, and the index must be created and maintained through an ingestion process.

scenes.title: AWS retrieval stores: choose by data and search needs
scenes.narration: This slide compares four possible AWS retrieval stores. Rather than memorize one universal answer, read each column and its intended workload. On the far left, Amazon OpenSearch Service combines vector similarity search with full-text search and analytics. The icons for documents, images and other content feeding the search engine illustrate its search-oriented design. If your application needs rich search features over a large distributed index, OpenSearch is a sensible candidate. Next, Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL is a managed relational database with extensions suitable for vector search. The table icon and vector extension label show why it may fit an application that already keeps its business records in PostgreSQL and wants semantic search alongside relational queries. The green third column is Amazon S3 Vectors. It stores and queries vector embeddings in vector indexes, with an emphasis on durable, scalable vector storage. Do not confuse this with simply putting PDFs into an ordinary S3 bucket. Finally, Neptune Analytics is shown with connected graph nodes. It is designed for graph relationships and can support graph-based retrieval, including GraphRAG configurations where appropriate. Consider questions about connections between entities, not just matching similar paragraphs. The decision cards at the bottom summarize the four choices: existing relational application suggests evaluating Aurora, search-rich workloads suggest OpenSearch, a vector storage requirement suggests S3 Vectors, and relationship-rich knowledge graphs suggest Neptune Analytics. One caution matters for architecture decisions: model compatibility, Regions, supported Knowledge Bases integrations, latency and pricing vary. These four products are not automatically drop-in replacements for one another, and none is guaranteed to be the fastest or cheapest.

scenes.title: Knowledge Base data sources: choose the supported path
scenes.narration: This slide has two large horizontal sections, and the difference between them matters. Start with the upper blue Managed Knowledge Base. The left-hand connector grid shows examples such as Amazon S3, SharePoint, Confluence, Google Drive, OneDrive and a Web Crawler. The goal is to authorize supported sources while AWS manages the connector operation. Follow the numbered stages across the top: first authorize access to source documents; second choose what to ingest and how often to synchronize; third parse the content and split it into chunks; fourth generate embeddings; and fifth retrieve relevant content with source metadata. The example retrieval card includes a source location and last-synchronized date, which are useful when checking whether an answer relies on current information. Now move to the lower purple Customer-managed Knowledge Base section. Here you can use S3 or build your own ingestion connector, but your team owns more of the connector infrastructure and synchronization. Its five stages are similar, yet the operational responsibility is different. Look closely at the yellow legacy-connector warning. The slide states that after September thirtieth, twenty twenty-six, new customer-managed connectors for Confluence, SharePoint, Salesforce and Web Crawler cannot be created, though existing connectors continue to work. That restriction is specific to the customer-managed path shown, not a claim that every managed connector disappeared. This is why you must confirm current AWS documentation, Region and product mode before planning a deployment. Finally, neither a connector nor a document citation automatically solves access control. Use appropriate source permissions, application authorization and data governance so users do not receive content they are not allowed to see.

scenes.title: RAG use cases: answers from your sources
scenes.narration: Here are three real situations in which retrieval-augmented generation can be useful. Read the three top panels from left to right. The first is customer support, illustrated by the headset. A customer asks, 'How do I set up my device?' RAG retrieves a passage from the Product Setup Guide mentioning powering on the device and connecting it to the network. The answer summarizes those steps and cites the guide. This is especially useful when product documentation changes faster than the foundation model's training data. The middle panel is legal research. The question asks what a document says about data retention. The retrieved excerpt references Section four point two of an internal legal document. The resulting answer points back to that section; the note below requires legal expert review before relying on it. The right panel is healthcare question answering. A clinician asks what the latest approved guidance says about treatment options. The system retrieves a relevant clinical guideline and produces a sourced summary. Notice the prominent purple warning: a qualified clinician must review the result and patient information must remain protected. A citation alone is not a medical decision. At the bottom, the four-step strip summarizes the shared architecture for all three cases: a user asks, the system retrieves matching content, the retrieved material is supplied to the AI model, and the model generates a grounded answer. The lower-right clock emphasizes freshness. Results can only reflect information that has been synchronized and retrieved. The useful habit across all three cases is to inspect the actual source, verify important claims and evaluate whether the final response meets the task's safety and quality requirements.
